content: Pickling, also referred to as brining or corning, is a method of food preservation that involves either anaerobic fermentation in a saltwater solution (brine) to produce lactic acid or marinating and storing food in an acidic solution, typically vinegar (acetic acid). The preserved food resulting from this process is called a pickle. This technique imparts a salty or sour flavor to the food. The acidity level, often around pH 4.6, is sufficient to inhibit the growth of most spoilage-causing bacteria. Pickling can extend the shelf life of perishable foods for several months. Antimicrobial herbs and spices, such as mustard, garlic, cinnamon, or cloves, are frequently added to enhance flavor and preservation. In cases where the food has adequate moisture content, a pickling brine can be created by simply adding dry salt. For example, sauerkraut and Korean kimchi are made by salting vegetables to draw out excess water. The natural fermentation process, facilitated by lactic acid bacteria at room temperature, generates the necessary acidity. Alternatively, some pickles are prepared by immersing vegetables directly in vinegar. Unlike canning, pickling (including fermentation) does not require the food to be completely sterile before sealing. The final flavor and microbial profile of the pickled product are influenced by factors such as the acidity or salinity of the solution, fermentation temperature, and the exclusion of oxygen. When both salt concentration and temperature are low, Leuconostoc mesenteroides predominates, producing a mixture of acids, alcohol, and aromatic compounds. At higher temperatures, Lactobacillus plantarum becomes dominant, primarily producing lactic acid. Many pickles begin with Leuconostoc and transition to Lactobacillus as acidity increases. Historically, pickling was developed as a means to preserve food for off-season use and long voyages, particularly by sea. Salted pork and beef were staples for sailors before the advent of steam engines. While originally intended for preservation, pickles are also enjoyed for their unique flavors. Additionally, pickling can enhance the nutritional value of food by introducing B vitamins produced by bacteria. Popularity of Pickles Around the World Asia East Asia: In China, a wide variety of pickled vegetables are popular, including radish, Chinese cabbage (notably suan cai, la bai cai, pao cai, and Tianjin preserved vegetables), zha cai, chili peppers, and cucumbers. Japanese tsukemono (pickled foods) include takuan (daikon), umeboshi (ume plum), gari and beni shoga (ginger), turnip, cucumber, and Chinese cabbage. Korean kimchi is typically made from pickled Chinese cabbage. South Asia: In Sri Lanka, traditional pickles called achcharu are made from slices of carrots, onions, ground dates, mustard mixed with pepper, crushed ginger, garlic, and vinegar, often prepared in a clay pot. Southeast Asia: Indonesian acar is commonly made from sliced or diced cucumber, carrot, bird's eye chilies, shallots, and seasoned with vinegar, sugar, and salt. Sometimes, fruits like papaya and pineapple are added. In the Philippines, pickles called achara are made from green papaya slices, shallots, garlic cloves, and vinegar. In Vietnam, pickles known as cải chua (sour vegetables) are often made from mustard greens. Europe Turkey: Pickles, known as turşu, are made from various vegetables, roots, and fruits such as peppers, cucumbers, Armenian cucumbers (acur), cabbage, tomatoes, eggplants, carrots, turnips, beets, green almonds, and green plums, often flavored with spices. Balkans: In Albania, Bulgaria, and Serbia, mixed pickles called turshi are a traditional appetizer, often served with rakia. Popular pickled items include green tomatoes, cucumbers, carrots, bell peppers, eggplants, and sauerkraut. Romania: Common pickles include beets, cucumbers, green tomatoes (gogonele), carrots, cabbage, bell peppers, melons, mushrooms, and cauliflower. Russia: Popular pickled foods include beets, mushrooms, tomatoes, cabbage, cucumbers, ramsons, garlic, eggplants (often stuffed with julienned carrots), custard squash, and even watermelon. Pickled herring and rollmops are common in Scandinavia, and salmon may also be brine-pickled. United Kingdom: Pickled onions and pickled eggs are often sold in pubs and fish-and-chip shops. Pickled beetroot, walnuts, and gherkins, as well as condiments like Branston Pickle and piccalilli, are typically served with pork pies, cold meats, or a ploughman’s lunch. Ukraine: Common garden produce is often pickled with dill for winter consumption. Ingredients like salt, dill, currant leaves, and garlic are used to give tomatoes and cucumbers a distinctive flavor after storage in a cool, dark place. Italy: Giardiniera, a dish of pickled vegetables such as onions, carrots, celery, and cauliflower, is popular. Italian giardiniera differs from the American condiment of the same name. Middle East In Iran and many Arab countries like Lebanon and Egypt, pickles (called mekhallal in Arabic, hamutzim in Hebrew, or torshi in Persian) are served with nearly every meal. Common varieties include turnips, peppers, green olives, cucumbers, beets, cabbage, lemons, and cauliflower. North America In the United States and Canada, the pickle market is dominated by pickled cucumbers (commonly referred to simply as pickles), olives, and sauerkraut. However, pickles popular in other nations, such as pickled tomatoes, are also available, particularly in New York City delicatessens. Giardiniera, a mix of pickled peppers, celery, and olives, is a popular condiment in Chicago, often served with Italian beef sandwiches. Pickled eggs are common in Michigan's Upper Peninsula, while pickled okra is popular in the southern United States. In Mexico, pickled chili peppers, particularly jalapeños and serranos, are often prepared with onions, carrots, and herbs as common condiments. Other Commonly Pickled Foods Vegetables: Ginger, lotus root, garlic, asparagus, onion, radish, green beans, and eggplant. Capers and olives: These are typically served pickled in the West, unlike the salt-cured versions preferred in the Orient.
